title: Tuning and the open strings
description: Lock in standard-tuning names, the 5-5-5-4-5 gaps, and the fret-matching method.

cards.front: What is tuning?
cards.back: The set of pitches your open strings produce.

cards.front: Name the six open strings from string 6 to string 1.
cards.back: E A D G B E.

cards.front: Give the sounding octave number for each open string, 6 to 1.
Why are the open strings called anchors?
cards.back: They are six notes you can name with no counting. Every fretted note is found by counting half steps from one of them.

cards.front: What is the half-step spacing between neighboring open strings, 6→5→4→3→2→1?
cards.back: 5-5-5-4-5. Four perfect fourths and one major third (strings 3 to 2).

cards.front: Name the interval between each neighboring open-string pair.
Why is there a major third between strings 3 and 2?
cards.back: Standard tuning is mostly fourths so chords and scales fit under the hand. The G-to-B major third (4 half steps) keeps the highest strings within easy reach of the lower ones.

cards.front: Is standard tuning a law of music?
cards.back: No. It is a convention. Drop D, open G, DADGAD and others rearrange the gaps, and every shape shifts.

cards.front: What does “Eddie Ate Dynamite…” not tell you?
cards.back: It only recalls the six names. It says nothing about the 5-5-5-4-5 spacing you use to navigate between strings.

cards.front: Same fret, next higher string (lower number): how many half steps up?
cards.back: 5 half steps, except strings 3 to 2, which is 4.

cards.front: A note on string 6 matches the next thinner string how many frets lower?
cards.back: Five frets lower (string 6 fret 5 = open string 5), except across G to B, where it is four frets lower.

cards.front: Which fret on string 6 matches open string 5?
cards.back: Fret 5. Both are A.

cards.front: Which fret on string 5 matches open string 4?
cards.back: Fret 5. Both are D.

cards.front: Which fret on string 4 matches open string 3?
cards.back: Fret 5. Both are G.

cards.front: Which fret on string 3 matches open string 2? Why is it not 5?
cards.back: Fret 4. Strings 3 to 2 are a major third (4 half steps), not a fourth.

cards.front: Which fret on string 2 matches open string 1?
cards.back: Fret 5. Both are E.

cards.front: Add the five open-string gaps. Why must the total be 24?
cards.back: 5 + 5 + 5 + 4 + 5 = 24 half steps = two octaves, from open string 6 (E2) to open string 1 (E4).

cards.front: What is beating when you tune two strings together?
cards.back: A slow wobble when two pitches are close but not equal. The slower the beats, the closer the match. Beats vanish when the pitches match.

cards.front: What is the standard reference pitch, and why does “in tune with itself” still matter?
cards.back: A4 = 440 Hz. A guitar can be in tune with itself but still flat or sharp against a piano or recording, so you tune to an external reference, then check strings against each other.

cards.front: Approximate frequencies of the six open strings?
What interval do you hear between open 5 and 4? Between open 3 and 2?
cards.back: Open 5 to 4 is a perfect fourth. Open 3 to 2 is a major third — slightly narrower, the audible 4-half-step gap.

cards.front: Find A on strings 6, 5, 4, and 3 using only frets 0–7.
cards.back: String 6 fret 5, open string 5, string 4 fret 7, string 3 fret 2.

cards.front: In the key of A, which open strings are the root, fourth, and fifth?
cards.back: Open A is the root, open D is the fourth, open E is the fifth.

cards.front: Why do keys such as E, A, D, and G feel idiomatic on guitar?
cards.back: Their open strings double as roots, fifths, and other chord tones, so open-position chords ring fully.
